sources.text: August 11, 2026 Combustible non-tobacco nicotine analog cigarettes Filed under: Tobacco/Nicotine — Tags: E-cigarettes , smoking , vaping — mtaffe @ 5:41 pm Seidenberg and colleagues have published an “Industry Watch” piece in Tobacco Control which alerts us to the latest industry ploy to addict more people to nicotine and related analog compounds. As they conclude “ To our knowledge, Choice Smokes is the first combustible product made with a nicotine analogue. The availability of products that undermine tobacco control regulations raises concerns about potential health and addiction risks to consumers. “ In a prior entry I mentioned that we have a new research interest in the effects of 6-methyl nicotine (6-MN) , which has appeared in both e-cigarette liquids and oral pouch products in recent years. This is a new version of the old analog strategy, whereby entities that seek to profit from psychoactive drugs attempt to evade legal regulation of their market. In the case of Schedule I drugs such as various amphetamine analogs in the 1980s, and the synthetic cannabinoids (“Spice”, “K2”, etc) and substituted cathinones (“bath salts”) in the 2010s, the goal was to evade legal prohibition. To large extent the proliferation of amphetamine and cathinone analogs were attempts to get effects similar to MDMA (Ecstasy) in a drug which was not illegal to possess and sell. The synthetic cannabinoid products featured otherwise inert plant materials adulterated with any of a number of full-agonist cannabinoids in an attempt to get a cannabis-like (delta9-tetrahydrocannabinol) effects from products that were legal to sell and possess. This new analog strategy is slightly different in the sense that nicotine is legal to possess, use and sell. However, it is a regulated industry, with the FDA recently empowered to decide if new products may enter the market. The nicotine industry also is subject to a host of taxes as well as restrictions on the marketing of their products. In this case it is quite obvious that the analog strategy is being used to evade all of these things, with an obvious primary goal of keeping the FDA from disallowing any new products. In the case of nicotine pouches and even e-cigarette liquids there is some plausible argument to reduced harm relative to inhaling the smoke from combusted tobacco in a traditional cigarette. This new product, however, abandons even that conceit since it is a combustible plant material infused in some way with 6-MN. The website for “CHOICE by Signature Brands” asserts repeatedly that this is a non-tobacco, non-nicotine product. It also talks a lot about the “ritual” of traditional smoking and makes oblique health claims “ eliminating the harmful substances associated with tobacco products ” without any evidence their “ersatz” cigarettes do not contain other equally harmful substances. The website is also forthright about these products avoiding tobacco taxes and regulations. The website is not so forthright about the active ingredient. It refers to “Novara” with a trademark label and describes it as “ providing the effect, presence, and balance that adult smokers seek in their ritual. ” Ritual, you will recognize, is the old, old strategy of the tobacco industry to claim that their products were not addictive , but merely a harmless “ habit ” preferred by some individuals. The website does brag about how the lower cost compared with “traditional options” is “ making it easy to enjoy daily “. Daily. Yes of course they know this is an addictive product. Over on the FAQ page , they state that “ NOVARA is a proprietary formulated nicotine substitute which delivers the same pleasure “. This is a curious lack of transparency give how open they are about their intentions to evade taxes and regulatory oversight. Luckily Seidenberg and colleagues have snooped out the website page on Quality and Compliance , which is not directly navigable from any other part of the website that I can find. This page has at present links to two opinions from legal consultation. A letter from one Barry M. Boren reviews the current regulatory environment. It states that the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act of 2009 covers only tobacco products, mentions the “deeming” of 2016 whereby the FDA asserted jurisdiction over non-tobacco products containing nicotine derived from tobacco and the 2022 Congressional expansion to nicotine of any source. It then concludes that nicotine analogues are not subject to FDA oversight without mentioning which analog is in the Signature Brands’ product. A concurring letter from Allen F Bennett , of Bennett Intellectual Property law firm, gives us the specifics. It starts, memo-like with “Re: 6-Methyl-Nicotine Comparison to Nicotine”. It then goes on to summarize the chemical differences of 6-MN from nicotine and makes an argument that Congress knowingly chose not to include any nicotine analogs, most specifically 6-MN in any of its authorizations of the FDA to regulate nicotine products. So thanks to Seidenberg and colleagues we now know that the active chemical in this product is 6-MN. About which very little appears in the scientific literature. That which is available suggests that 6-MN will be quite similar to nicotine in effect with perhaps only minor differences in potency. These products are as yet completely unregulated. The legal opinions rendered suggest the industry is free to market these as they wish, sell to children and avoid paying anything other than basic sales taxes. This particular product already comes in a menthol variety, a pharmacologically active ingredient that serves to enhance the detrimental effects of nicotine, thereby evading any regional restrictions on menthol flavorants in tobacco cigarettes or e-cigarette products. It is very likely to be another long policy fight to bring 6-MN and other nicotine analogs under the regulatory constraints that have been hard won to diminish the health harms of tobacco and nicotine. The first step is awareness of these products and awareness that the analogs are likely to be just as harmful as nicotine. Seidenberg, Andrew and Jabba, Sairam and Goniewicz, Maciej L. and Jordt, Sven E, Combustible Tobacco-Free Cigarettes Containing a Nicotine Analogue – a Dangerous Design to Counter Smoking Regulations? Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6868879 or http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6868879 Leave a Comment August 3, 2026 Exploring the role of cannabis in the rewarding effects of exercise Filed under: Cannabis , Exercise , Opiates — mtaffe @ 4:00 pm The public discussion of cannabis in the context of physical activity has mostly been dominated by arguing over whether it should be banned from top level athletics as a performance enhancing drug. Occasionally there are cases of top level performers being drummed out of professional sports due to repeated positive tests for cannabis, with the implication that they have a cannabis use disorder of significance. Often, these discussions touch on cultural factors of the sports in question, such as snowboarding and alpine skiing. The idea being that people who snowboard or ski also happen to be people who enjoy recreational cannabis and this becomes part of the culture without any specific causal interaction. I became aware in my younger years that one of those sports was cycling. My local road cycling club (this was prior to the expansion of mountain biking), the Greasy Gonzos, was famous for taking weed breaks during their Wednesday night rides. Those of us who were teens involved in the sports of cross country running and Nordic ski racing were more than a little nonplussed by the seeming incompatibility of sparking up joints in the middle of aerobic workouts. Somewhat later, during the Golden Age of mountain biking I was therefore slightly more prepared for the riders that showed up completely baked for the Wednesday night Cantina rides . Or the ones who brought out the joints at the Snow Summit race series . This all appeared to me to be more of a cultural association than anything specific about cannabis use before, during or after exercise. Particularly since these experiences were all before I became interested in the reinforcing properties of drugs and the behavioral effects of cannabis in the professional research sphere. It is hardly news that one of the more consistent recommendations for improving various aspects of health is to get more exercise, nor that some individuals struggle to maintain exercise programs. Interestingly, a targeted pro-exercise intervention found increased days per week of exercise in cannabis users versus non-users ( YorkWilliams et al., 2020 ). In addition, a survey of cannabis users found that 87% used cannabis shortly before exercise and 26% used cannabis during exercise ( Ogle et al., 2022 ). Of these, 51% reported using cannabis with aerobic machines and 44% with weightlifting and overall, some 66% of respondents said cannabis helped them to enjoy exercise more . This is intriguing, given our work from which we have an operating conclusion that 3,4-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the dominant psychoactive constituent of cannabis, reduces opioid drug self-administration by enhancing the reinforcing effects of a given amount of heroin or oxycodone . Two-thirds of exercising cannabis users in that survey appeared to be saying that cannabis enhanced the reinforcing effects of exercise. This leads to an expanded interest in the laboratory. I am pleased to report that the Taffe lab has been awarded a two year Pilot grant from the Center for Medicinal Cannabis Research (CMCR) to further investigate how THC may increase the rewarding effects of exercise in rats. As background, the CMCR grant program currently credits funding derived from Proposition 64: The Adult Use of Marijuana Act which was voted in by the voters of California and went into effect in 2016. One of the specific parts of the text of the initiative stated: Revenue from the two taxes will be deposited in a new California Marijuana Tax Fund. First, the revenue will be used to cover costs of administrating and enforcing the measure. Next, it will be distributed to drug research, treatment, and enforcement, including: $2 million per year to the UC San Diego Center for Medicinal Cannabis Research to study medical marijuana. In relationship to a prior observation on this blog, we are happy to once again respond to the request of the taxpayers to generate scientific information on topics considered to be of interest to them. Our Aims for this project are Specific Aim 1: Does low-dose THC accelerate the escalation of wheel activity in rats? Anyone who has visited a pet store that sells hamsters, mice and/or rats knows that small rodents will run on an activity wheel when given the opportunity. This was formalized long ago in the behaviorism / experimental psychology literature by people such as David Premack who showed that the opportunity to use a wheel functioned as a reinforcer. That is, lever pressing behavior would be increased if it was followed by the opportunity to run on a wheel. This line of research has been most recently pursued by Terry Belke and colleagues . Our experiments under this Aim will determine if vaping low to moderate doses of THC facilitates the rewarding effects of wheel activity. Specific Aim 2: Does low-dose THC enhance the reinforcing effects of wheel activity in rats? This Aim is related to prior work from the lab in which we showed that activity on a wheel diminished the intravenous self-administration of stimulant drugs. We first demonstrated that when rats are given concurrent access to a wheel within the operant chamber they self-administer less methamphetamine (Miller et al., 2012). We also found that wheel access in the ~day before a session reduces self-administration of methamphetamine, 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and methylone (Aarde, Miller et al., 2015). We have shown that wheel activity diminishes across the first 2-3 weeks of acquisition of either methamphetamine or MDPV self administration in male rats (Miller et al., 2012; Aarde, Huang et al., 2015), something that does not affect female rats self-administering alpha-PVP (Javadi-Paydar, et al. 2018). We’re grateful to the CMCR for supporting our work on the rewarding properties of exercise. This proposal was motivated in part, as I mentioned before , by a recognition that the opioid crisis was not agnostic to age. That is, the famous opioid-related deaths graph you are used to seeing does not look the same for all age brackets. This graph from another CDC report breaks down all overdose deaths from 1999-2015 by the age of the decedent. The steepest rate of increase was seen in the 55-65 year old cohort, i.e., middle aged individuals. The upshot is that rates which looked more like those of 65+ year olds and 15-24 year olds rose away from these lowest risk groups to cluster with the 25-44 year olds. Interestingly, the overdose rates for those approaching middle age, 45-54 years of age had already risen to the highest risk of all around 2006-2015. There are many possible reasons for the increased overdose in middle age, including a host of social and economic factors. My subfield of science, in many ways, works to take those unique human factors out of the equation by using animal models. In our case, rats. This subfield has been very industrious at using, for example, the intravenous self-administration approach to determine quite a bit about the substance misuse disorders. Another motivation for our grant proposal was, however, my realization that there are very few reports on even the basics of self-administration in rats in middle age or older. One exception is Bongiovanni et al., 2021 which reported 20-24 month old rats self-administer less morphine than 2-4 month old rats. Actually, this is the exception. The only paper published on later life intravenous self-administration of opioids in rats. At least as far as I have found. I can’t say why with any authority. Scientists have been using this model of rat intravenous self-administration since Weeks published an initial report in 1962 . There have been hundreds, maybe even thousands, of labs that use this procedure. You would think that at least several someones, somewhere, for some reason would have tried to conduct a study of opioid self-administration in older adult rats. Especially as we started hearing assertions over the years that surely the prescription opioid misuse crisis was driven by over prescription of oxycodone for pain. Post-surgical pain, back pain, minor trauma pain. None of which health conditions associate cleanly or uniquely with adolescence or young adulthood. So you would think at some point there would have been some attempts. Middle aged male rats self-administer less heroin. My best guess is that this is because it costs money to age rats up in the lab for a year and nobody wanted to take that on for minimal obvious gain. When they could be running two, three or more cohorts of rats for the same amount of time and money to house them. Second guess is that since most problematic substance use starts much earlier in life, there was no real motivation to study older animals. With respect to the age-related overdose rates, well, it took a lot of time for my subfield to start doing research on oxycodone after the association of that drug with overdose was being recognized. Third guess, well, we ourselves had some concerns on the practical and tactical level. The health of older animals. Their response to the surgical implantation of catheters. Their timeline for completing experiments versus the onset of significant later life health concerns (as mentioned, most of them will not live past 24 months). Their ability to learn, i.e. to make the association between pressing on a lever and the way the infusion of drug made them feel. Some of our work on this project could be viewed as mere methods development and validation. To show peers in the subfield that it is possible to study intravenous self-administration in middle aged rats*. We were fortunate enough to secure funding with the explicit understanding we would have to age animals up in the laboratory. For a year. Paying a per diem rate to do nothing with them.
